By the end you’ll know how to capture useful events, spot hot collections, and trace slow operations for remediation.

screens.title: Auditing: What it records and why it matters
screens.narratorSegment: Auditing is the systematic capture of database events that describe who performed an action, from where, and what the result was. In MongoDB Enterprise this includes authentication attempts, authorization failures, DDL operations such as creating or dropping collections and indexes, and DML operations like inserts and updates when you choose to log them. The audit log records useful fields such as the authenticated user, source IP, command executed, and the outcome. This level of detail is essential when you need to perform forensic analysis after an incident or to meet compliance requirements that demand an immutable record of access. A concrete example: if an unauthorized script attempts repeated logins and triggers authorization failures, the audit trail will show the username, source IP, and timestamps needed to investigate. A common misconception is that auditing is only for security; it is also valuable operationally to discover who changed schema or indexes and when. One pitfall to avoid is enabling auditing without planning for log rotation and storage—audit files can grow rapidly. Key takeaway: audit selectively, choose the right filters and destinations, and pair audit data with monitoring metrics so you can answer both who did something and what effect it had on system health.

keyIdea.title: Auditing defined
keyIdea.text: Audit logs record detailed events for accountability and troubleshooting; plan storage and filtering to keep logs useful.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.3 › Auditing: What it records
Definition

What an audit trail contains

  • Authenticated user identity and roles.
  • Source IP address and connection metadata.
  • Command executed and its parameters.
  • Operation outcome: success or failure with error details.
Analogy
Think of an audit log as a building security camera plus an entry log: it shows who badge-swiped, when, and whether access was granted.
Example
A failed authentication flood from one IP will appear as multiple authenticate events with the same source and timestamps. Investigators can trace the username and origin to determine if it was a brute-force attempt or a misconfigured client.
Common Mistake
Turning on broad auditing without filters or rotation causes huge files and operational risk from disk exhaustion.
Pro Tip
Use auditLog.filter to focus on authentication and authorization initially, then expand as needed for compliance.
Key Takeaway

Audits give accountability and context. Capture carefully, filter intelligently, and rotate logs to avoid operational costs.

screens.title: MongoDB native auditing framework
screens.narratorSegment: MongoDB Enterprise provides a native auditing framework that captures a configurable set of events. You can choose to record authentication attempts, authorization checks, DDL changes like index creations or drops, and selected DML commands. The audit subsystem supports several destinations: console, syslog, or JSON files on disk. For production you typically write JSON to a file or forward to syslog for central ingestion. Filters let you limit what is recorded; a good example is auditing authentication and authorization events but excluding a trusted service account. The filter language accepts MongoDB style query expressions so you can include or exclude events by type, user, or command parameters. A concrete configuration example is placing auditLog settings in mongod. conf to write JSON to /var/log/mongodb/audit. json. Remember that auditing is an Enterprise feature; if you are using community builds you will not have this capability. Finally, plan for log rotation and archival: audit files are authoritative for investigations and must be retained according to your compliance policy. Misconception check: audit logs are not a replacement for monitoring metrics — combine both to answer who acted and what performance impact resulted.

keyIdea.title: Framework essentials
keyIdea.text: Events, destinations, and filters define what is captured and where. Use filters to reduce noise and files/syslog for production ingestion.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.3 › MongoDB native auditing
Events & Destinations
Events include authenticate, authorize, createIndex, dropCollection, and optional DML command logging. Destinations include console, syslog, and file in JSON format for downstream analysis.
  • JSON files: structured, easy to parse and archive.
  • Syslog: integrate with centralized log systems.
  • Console: useful for development but not for production.
Filter
Use auditLog.filter to include or exclude events. Filters reduce noise and storage by focusing on critical event types or specific users.
Production advice
  • Prefer file or syslog destinations in production.
  • Plan log rotation and archival before enabling broad auditing.
  • Combine audit logs with a SIEM or log aggregator for alerting and search.
Note
Auditing is an Enterprise feature. Ensure your build supports auditLog before relying on it.
Key Takeaway

Choose filters and destinations intentionally; audit for critical events and retain logs per policy.

screens.title: Enable auditing in mongod.conf
screens.narratorSegment: Here is a practical configuration pattern used to enable audit logging to a JSON file. You place an auditLog section in mongod. conf and select the destination, format, path, and a filter expression. The filter is written in a MongoDB query-like form so you can include authentication events or any other event types you care about. A concrete snippet will write JSON to /var/log/mongodb/audit. json and filter for authenticate events, excluding a superAdmin account in this example. Notice two operational points: first, the file path must be writable by the mongod process, and second, ensure rotation is handled outside of MongoDB, for example by logrotate, because audit files can grow quickly. Also remember auditing is Enterprise-only. Misconception check: adding auditLog does not make your system secure by itself; it only records actions. Combine it with access controls, monitoring, and retention policies. In the lab we will add this to mongod. conf, start mongod with authentication enabled, and observe the JSON audit file as we produce activity. Enable auditing in mongod.conf means add auditlog to mongod.conf, select destination, format, path, and use filters to target important events.. In practical terms, a guarded, practical example for file-based json audit logs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Add auditLog to mongod.conf, select destination, format, path, and use filters to target important events.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.3 › Enable auditing in mongod.conf
Code Walkthrough
# mongod.conf snippet for Auditing (Enterprise feature) auditLog: destination: file format: JSON path: /var/log/mongodb/audit.json filter: '{ atype: "authenticate", "param.user": { $ne: "superAdmin" } }' # Or for all auth and authorization events: # filter: '{ $or: [ { atype: "authenticate" }, { atype: "authorize" } ] }'
Operational Notes
  • Ensure the mongod user can write to the audit file path.
  • Use external log rotation to prevent disk exhaustion.
  • Start with focused filters to avoid excessive volume.
Example explanation
This example audits authentication events and skips entries from a superAdmin account. In practice you might invert this to audit all except trusted service accounts, or audit specific DDL operations for compliance.
Checklist before enabling
  1. Confirm Enterprise build supports auditing.
  2. Choose destination and ensure write permission.
  3. Plan rotation and retention policy.
Key Takeaway

Audit configuration goes in mongod.conf. Verify permissions, rotate logs, and start with targeted filters.

screens.title: Using mongostat for real-time metrics
screens.narratorSegment: Mongostat is a lightweight command-line utility that prints a one-line-per-interval snapshot of a MongoDB instance’s activity. It reports operation counts — insert, query, update, delete, getmore, and command — along with network bytes in/out, number of connections, memory usage, and page faults. The output updates every second by default, giving you immediate visibility into spikes and sudden changes. A simple command to connect with authentication looks like the provided example; you’ll run mongostat while generating load to see the values change. Concretely, if you run many inserts you will see the insert column jump and network bytes out increase. A common misconception is that mongostat replaces profiling; it doesn’t. Profiling gives per-query detail while mongostat is for quick operational health checks. Use mongostat to detect sudden spikes and then switch to more detailed tools or logs to diagnose the root cause. In practice, start mongostat first, reproduce an issue or run a load script, and watch which counters move. That tells you where to dig next. Using mongostat for real-time metrics means mongostat gives live operation rates and system counters — useful for spotting sudden spikes and confirming workload changes.. In practical terms, what mongostat reports and how to read it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.3 › Using mongostat
Command
mongostat --host localhost --port 27017 --authenticationDatabase admin -u superAdmin -p superSecurePassword
Key columns to watch: insert, query, update, delete, getmore, command, network bytes in/out, and connections. Watch for sudden jumps and sustained high values to identify pressure points.
Misconception
mongostat does not show per-collection details. Use mongotop or profiling for more granular insight.
Example output (simplified)
insert query update delete getmore command network_in network_out conn 0 5 0 0 0 2 1kB 2kB 12 10 20 0 0 0 4 10kB 15kB 35
If you trigger inserts, the insert column and network_out will grow. Use that signal to identify which operation class is causing load.
Key Takeaway

Use mongostat for rapid, live observation of operation rates and system counters to spot spikes.

screens.title: Using mongotop to find hot collections
screens.narratorSegment: Mongotop reports how much time a MongoDB instance spends reading and writing for each collection. Unlike mongostat, which is operation-focused, mongotop is collection-focused and shows you where time is being spent. This helps you find hot collections that may need indexing, schema changes, or sharding. The standard invocation is similar to mongostat and updates periodically. In practice you run mongotop while exercising the application and look for collections with consistently high read or write time percentages. For example, if a collection stores session data and shows persistently high write time, you may decide to move session writes to a different tier or partition the collection. A common misconception is to equate high throughput with inefficiency; mongotop focuses on time spent, not raw operations per second. High time means the server is spending C P U or input and output servicing that collection, which can lead to latency for other workloads. Use mongotop findings to guide index creation, query optimization, or architectural changes like sharding. Using mongotop to find hot collections means mongotop shows time spent per collection to reveal hotspots; use it to prioritize indexing and partitioning work.. In practical terms, measure read/write time by collection to identify hotspots. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.3 › Using mongotop
Command
mongotop --host localhost --port 27017 --authenticationDatabase admin -u superAdmin -p superSecurePassword
Mongotop reports collection names and time spent reading and writing per interval. Look for collections with sustained percentages of time to identify real bottlenecks.
Misconception
High operation count does not always imply high time. Mongotop measures time, which better reflects resource contention.
Example output (abbreviated)
ns total read write testdb.testcollection 10ms 8ms 2ms testdb.sessions 200ms 0ms 200ms
In this sample the sessions collection consumes 200ms of write time, indicating a write hotspot worth investigating.
Key Takeaway

Use mongotop to identify which collections consume time and should be the focus for optimization.

screens.title: Understanding mongod.log and slow queries
screens.narratorSegment: The server log, commonly mongod. log, is a rich record of server lifecycle messages, connection events, replication changes, errors, and slow operations. Slow query logging is particularly important: MongoDB records commands that exceed slowOpThresholdMs so you can find and optimize long-running queries. Developers should watch for slowms entries, which include the query, execution time, and stack of operations. A concrete workflow: set a conservative slowOpThresholdMs to capture queries that you consider too slow for your environment, then reproduce problematic requests and inspect the log for the slowms entries. A common mistake is to leave the threshold too high and never log issues for small datasets during testing, or too low and flood logs with benign entries. Another frequent oversight is not combining logs with context from mongostat/mongotop: a slow query entry becomes more actionable when you can say it coincided with spikes in C P U or input and output. In short, tune slowOpThresholdMs for your workload, search mongod. log for slow query records, and use those records to guide index and schema changes. In practical terms, where to look and what slowopthresholdms controls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.3 › mongod.log and slow queries
What mongod.log contains
  • Server startup and shutdown events.
  • Connection and authentication messages.
  • Replication and election activity.
  • Slow query entries and errors.
Tuning
Adjust slowOpThresholdMs in mongod.conf to record queries that matter for your environment. For small test datasets you may need a low threshold to observe issues.
Example log excerpt
2024-01-01T12:00:00.000+00:00 WARNING [conn123] slowms: 125 command testdb.testcollection query: { data: /some_data/ } millis: 125
This entry shows the command, the execution time, and the millisecond duration. Use this to find expensive queries and inspect their explain plan.
Key Takeaway

screens.title: Run mongostat and mongotop concurrently
screens.narratorSegment: The core of this interactive lab is running mongostat and mongotop in parallel terminals while you generate workload from a third shell. Start mongostat to watch operation rates and overall counters, and start mongotop to see time spent per collection. Then, in the third terminal, run inserts, queries, and updates against testdb. testcollection. You will see the insert count rise in mongostat and collection time rise in mongotop. For example, running a loop of inserts will show an immediate jump in the insert column in mongostat and write time for testcollection in mongotop. Use these signals together: mongostat tells you which operation type increased, and mongotop shows which collection consumed time. A common pitfall is reading mongostat columns as absolute values rather than rates per interval. Remember the numbers reflect the activity during each sampling period. After observing changes, take a moment to correlate with the server log and audit file to see which authenticated user generated the events. This practice trains you to triage production incidents quickly by linking who did what with the observed performance impact. screens.title: Triggering a slow query and inspecting logs
screens.narratorSegment: In this step you will intentionally make a query slow so you can see how it appears in mongod. log and how to use that information to take action. Begin by dropping an index on the test collection. Then run a large, unindexed query such as a regex search or a filter on a non-indexed field. If your slowOpThresholdMs is not already low, temporarily lower it so the query is recorded for this small dataset. After running the query, open mongod. log and search for slowms or related entries; you will see the command and execution time recorded. That log entry gives the query shape and timing, which you can use to build an index or rewrite the query. A common misconception is that slow entries automatically mean bad indexing; sometimes the issue is high concurrency or input and output contention. Correlate the slowms entry with mongostat and mongotop output taken during the same interval to see whether C P U, memory, or a specific collection was the bottleneck. Your final action should be to create a compound index or restore the dropped index, then re-run the query and confirm the slowms entry disappears or falls below the threshold.

Commands

This entry shows the command and duration. Use the query shape to design an index that supports the filter or avoid regex where possible.

Use slow log entries to find expensive query shapes and validate fixes by re-testing after indexing or schema changes.

screens.title: Cloud Manager and Ops Manager overview

For example, Ops Manager can show a week-long C P U or replication lag trend and send an alert when latency thresholds are breached. screens.title: Log aggregation and rotation strategy
screens.narratorSegment: A production-ready auditing and monitoring strategy includes log aggregation and robust rotation. Aggregation means forwarding audit and server logs to a centralized system so you can search, correlate, and alert across many hosts. Systems like ELK, Splunk, or similar aggregators let you run queries over large volumes and create alerts for patterns such as repeated authorization failures. Rotation is equally important: audit files can grow rapidly, so use external rotation tools to compress and archive old files and prevent disk exhaustion. A simple pattern is to write audit logs to JSON files, run logrotate to rotate daily with compression, and ship rotated files to long-term storage or your SIEM. Misconception check: central aggregation does not replace local rotation; both are needed. Aggregation solves analysis and alerting, rotation solves storage and operational risk. Implement retention policies aligned with compliance needs. Together, these practices make audit trails useful, searchable, and safe to operate at scale. Log aggregation and rotation strategy means ship logs to a centralized system for analysis and alerting, and rotate/retain local logs to avoid storage issues.. In practical terms, collect logs centrally and rotate to protect storage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll establish why auditing and monitoring are essential to running a healthy, secure MongoDB deployment. Auditing gives you a tamper-evident trail of who did what and when, which is crucial for security investigations and compliance. Monitoring provides real-time and historical visibility into resource use and query patterns so you can detect performance bottlenecks early. You will see concrete examples of the native MongoDB audit framework, learn how to configure auditLog in your mongod configuration, and use the command-line tools mongostat and mongotop to observe live activity. We’ll also practice a small lab: enabling authentication, running the monitoring tools in parallel terminals, generating load, and deliberately triggering a slow query to inspect the server log. Finally, we’ll point out common mistakes, like forgetting log rotation for audit files, and explain why enterprise tools such as Cloud Manager and Ops Manager matter for long-running production fleets. By the end you’ll know how to capture useful events, spot hot collections, and trace slow operations for remediation.

By the end of these screens you will be able to explain why auditing and monitoring are essential to security and performance, configure MongoDB’s native audit logging to capture key events, run and interpret mongostat and mongotop to observe real-time activity, and read mongod logs to find slow queries and errors. You will also be aware of production best practices such as audit log destinations, filtering to reduce noise, log rotation, and when to use enterprise tooling like Cloud Manager or Ops Manager for historical metrics and alerting. Each objective is paired with a short practical mnemonic or checkpoint so you can verify competency: configure a simple auditLog entry in mongod. conf, start mongostat and mongotop concurrently while generating workload, and locate a slow query entry in mongod. log after deliberately removing an index. These are practical, measurable skills that help you collaborate with operations teams and maintain application availability and compliance.

This 2×2 objective grid maps a practical progression: first you understand the concepts, then you configure them, next you apply tools to diagnose live behavior, and finally you review and remediate issues. Understanding covers the difference between auditing and monitoring and why each matters. Configuration includes the auditLog section in mongod. conf and choosing a destination and filters. Application covers using mongostat and mongotop to see operation rates and hot collections while you generate workload. Review includes reading mongod. log for slow queries, adjusting slowOpThresholdMs, and integrating logs with an aggregator. Each step builds a measurable skill: understanding tells you what to collect, configuring captures it safely, applying helps you discover problems, and reviewing verifies resolution. This mindset helps you collaborate with operators, avoid common mistakes like missing log rotation, and choose when to adopt enterprise tools for long-term observability.

Auditing is the systematic capture of database events that describe who performed an action, from where, and what the result was. In MongoDB Enterprise this includes authentication attempts, authorization failures, DDL operations such as creating or dropping collections and indexes, and DML operations like inserts and updates when you choose to log them. The audit log records useful fields such as the authenticated user, source IP, command executed, and the outcome. This level of detail is essential when you need to perform forensic analysis after an incident or to meet compliance requirements that demand an immutable record of access. A concrete example: if an unauthorized script attempts repeated logins and triggers authorization failures, the audit trail will show the username, source IP, and timestamps needed to investigate. A common misconception is that auditing is only for security; it is also valuable operationally to discover who changed schema or indexes and when. One pitfall to avoid is enabling auditing without planning for log rotation and storage—audit files can grow rapidly. Key takeaway: audit selectively, choose the right filters and destinations, and pair audit data with monitoring metrics so you can answer both who did something and what effect it had on system health.

MongoDB Enterprise provides a native auditing framework that captures a configurable set of events. You can choose to record authentication attempts, authorization checks, DDL changes like index creations or drops, and selected DML commands. The audit subsystem supports several destinations: console, syslog, or JSON files on disk. For production you typically write JSON to a file or forward to syslog for central ingestion. Filters let you limit what is recorded; a good example is auditing authentication and authorization events but excluding a trusted service account. The filter language accepts MongoDB style query expressions so you can include or exclude events by type, user, or command parameters. A concrete configuration example is placing auditLog settings in mongod. conf to write JSON to /var/log/mongodb/audit. json. Remember that auditing is an Enterprise feature; if you are using community builds you will not have this capability. Finally, plan for log rotation and archival: audit files are authoritative for investigations and must be retained according to your compliance policy. Misconception check: audit logs are not a replacement for monitoring metrics — combine both to answer who acted and what performance impact resulted.

Here is a practical configuration pattern used to enable audit logging to a JSON file. You place an auditLog section in mongod. conf and select the destination, format, path, and a filter expression. The filter is written in a MongoDB query-like form so you can include authentication events or any other event types you care about. A concrete snippet will write JSON to /var/log/mongodb/audit. json and filter for authenticate events, excluding a superAdmin account in this example. Notice two operational points: first, the file path must be writable by the mongod process, and second, ensure rotation is handled outside of MongoDB, for example by logrotate, because audit files can grow quickly. Also remember auditing is Enterprise-only. Misconception check: adding auditLog does not make your system secure by itself; it only records actions. Combine it with access controls, monitoring, and retention policies. In the lab we will add this to mongod. conf, start mongod with authentication enabled, and observe the JSON audit file as we produce activity. Enable auditing in mongod.conf means add auditlog to mongod.conf, select destination, format, path, and use filters to target important events.. In practical terms, a guarded, practical example for file-based json audit logs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Mongostat is a lightweight command-line utility that prints a one-line-per-interval snapshot of a MongoDB instance’s activity. It reports operation counts — insert, query, update, delete, getmore, and command — along with network bytes in/out, number of connections, memory usage, and page faults. The output updates every second by default, giving you immediate visibility into spikes and sudden changes. A simple command to connect with authentication looks like the provided example; you’ll run mongostat while generating load to see the values change. Concretely, if you run many inserts you will see the insert column jump and network bytes out increase. A common misconception is that mongostat replaces profiling; it doesn’t. Profiling gives per-query detail while mongostat is for quick operational health checks. Use mongostat to detect sudden spikes and then switch to more detailed tools or logs to diagnose the root cause. In practice, start mongostat first, reproduce an issue or run a load script, and watch which counters move. That tells you where to dig next. Using mongostat for real-time metrics means mongostat gives live operation rates and system counters — useful for spotting sudden spikes and confirming workload changes.. In practical terms, what mongostat reports and how to read it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Mongotop reports how much time a MongoDB instance spends reading and writing for each collection. Unlike mongostat, which is operation-focused, mongotop is collection-focused and shows you where time is being spent. This helps you find hot collections that may need indexing, schema changes, or sharding. The standard invocation is similar to mongostat and updates periodically. In practice you run mongotop while exercising the application and look for collections with consistently high read or write time percentages. For example, if a collection stores session data and shows persistently high write time, you may decide to move session writes to a different tier or partition the collection. A common misconception is to equate high throughput with inefficiency; mongotop focuses on time spent, not raw operations per second. High time means the server is spending C P U or input and output servicing that collection, which can lead to latency for other workloads. Use mongotop findings to guide index creation, query optimization, or architectural changes like sharding. The server log, commonly mongod. log, is a rich record of server lifecycle messages, connection events, replication changes, errors, and slow operations. Slow query logging is particularly important: MongoDB records commands that exceed slowOpThresholdMs so you can find and optimize long-running queries. Developers should watch for slowms entries, which include the query, execution time, and stack of operations. A concrete workflow: set a conservative slowOpThresholdMs to capture queries that you consider too slow for your environment, then reproduce problematic requests and inspect the log for the slowms entries. A common mistake is to leave the threshold too high and never log issues for small datasets during testing, or too low and flood logs with benign entries. Another frequent oversight is not combining logs with context from mongostat/mongotop: a slow query entry becomes more actionable when you can say it coincided with spikes in C P U or input and output. In short, tune slowOpThresholdMs for your workload, search mongod. log for slow query records, and use those records to guide index and schema changes. A production-ready auditing and monitoring strategy includes log aggregation and robust rotation. Aggregation means forwarding audit and server logs to a centralized system so you can search, correlate, and alert across many hosts. Systems like ELK, Splunk, or similar aggregators let you run queries over large volumes and create alerts for patterns such as repeated authorization failures. Rotation is equally important: audit files can grow rapidly, so use external rotation tools to compress and archive old files and prevent disk exhaustion. A simple pattern is to write audit logs to JSON files, run logrotate to rotate daily with compression, and ship rotated files to long-term storage or your SIEM. Misconception check: central aggregation does not replace local rotation; both are needed. Aggregation solves analysis and alerting, rotation solves storage and operational risk. Implement retention policies aligned with compliance needs. Together, these practices make audit trails useful, searchable, and safe to operate at scale. These three cards summarize core ideas you should carry forward. Each concept complements the others: audits tell you who did something, monitoring shows the effect on system health, and logs provide the detailed evidence of slow operations.
